topics.title: GRC 12.0 Architecture
topics.summary: How Access Control 12.0 is put together: frontend/backend layers, the systems that plug into it, and how the release history maps to what you'll find in a landscape.

blocks.text: GRC (Access Control) is a standalone ABAP system that sits in front of every SAP and non-SAP system whose access needs governing. End users reach it through a browser (NWBC or Fiori); the GRC/BASIS/security team reaches it through GUI + NWBC.

items.v: Web Dynpro page — support & light configuration
Configuration of GRC — owned jointly by Security, GRC and BASIS

blocks.title: Plug-in system
blocks.text: Any system connected to GRC is called a Plug-in system. On-premise plug-ins split into SAP (ABAP: S/4HANA, ECC, HR / JAVA: PI, PO, CRM, EP, MDG, Solman) and Non-SAP. Cloud plug-ins connect over web service/OData: Ariba, Concur, S/4HANA Cloud, SuccessFactors.
Rule of thumb: HR system → GRCPIERP. Everything else SAP ABAP (S/4HANA, ECC, BW) → GRCPINW. JAVA-stack systems (PI/PO/IDM/CRM/EP/MDG/Solman) need a main connector plus a subsequent connector.

blocks.title: Release History
rows: ABAP, Web Dynpro — not HANA compatible
ABAP, Web Dynpro — HANA compatible, SP22
ABAP, Web Dynpro, Fiori optional as front end, any DB — SP 23/24

blocks.text: DB compatibility: ECC 6.0 EHP1–6 is not HANA compatible; EHP7/8 is. S/4HANA always runs on HANA DB (mandatory) with Fiori as an optional front end.

topics.title: Post-Installation Steps (BASIS Pre-Checks)
topics.summary: The checklist to run right after GRC is installed — before any functional configuration starts. Mostly BASIS-owned; GRC team just needs to confirm each box is green.

blocks.text: These are checks, not configuration — done by BASIS, verified by the GRC consultant before functional work begins.

items.b: GRC system needs GRCFND_A. The plug-in system needs GRCPINW (S/4HANA/ECC/BW/CRM/GRC, non-HR) or GRCPIERP (SAP HR). Confirm versions via System → Status → Installed Software.

items.h: Check BC Sets for *GRAC* and *MSMP* are activated
items.b: T-code SCPR20, table SCPRACTST (SCPR*). Naming tells you the module: GRAC*REQUEST* → ARM, GRAC*ROLE* → BRM, GRAC*RA_RULESET* → ARA, GRAC*SPM* → EAM, GRC*MSMP* → ARM.
SPRO → GRC → General Settings → Activate applications in client. Ensure GRC-AC is Active.

SPRO → GRC → General Settings → Workflow → Perform Automatic Workflow Customizing (T-code SWU3). Every line — Maintain Runtime Environment, Maintain Definition Environment, Maintain Additional Settings and Services, Classify Tasks as General, Guided Procedures — should show green. If not, hand it to BASIS.

SPRO → GRC → General Settings → Workflow → Perform Task-Specific Customizing. Every task under GRC should be marked Background Task or General Task — an empty value should be set to General Task. If tasks are missing, or the GRC-AC folder / Assign Agents option isn't there, that's a BASIS fix via T-code PFTC.

blocks.text: DB rule of thumb: ECC system can run on any DB. S/4HANA system runs on HANA DB only.

topics.title: Connector Configuration
topics.summary: Wiring GRC to a plug-in system: the RFC prerequisite, naming conventions, and the five SPRO steps that turn a connection into something GRC can automate, analyze and provision against.

blocks.text: Prerequisite: a SYSTEM or COMMUNICATION type user ID in the plug-in system (S/4HANA/ECC/BW), assigned the RFC authorizations it needs — auth objects starting with S_RFC* give RFC access. All configuration below happens in the GRC system.

blocks.title: What the connector enables
blocks.text: S4HANA / BW → GRC AC lets GRC do automation user admin, risk analysis checks, and automation of role admin.
Path for steps 1–3: SPRO → GRC → Common Component Settings → Integration Framework.

items.b: Set up the RFC between the plug-in system and GRC. Always define the RFC connection name in CAPITAL letters. Example naming: GRP 350 (GRC) → ID7 800 (ECC) = ID7CLNT800. Transportable connections typically get a fixed name like ECCCLNT100 carried across GD1/GQ1/GP1; non-transportable ones are named per-system per-client (e.g. GD1 100 → ED1 100 = ED1CLNT100).

Source connector and logical port should match the target connector. Pick the connection type by target: ECC / S/4HANA On-Premise → SAP. S/4HANA Cloud → S4HANA. Non-SAP → WS (webservice). JAVA systems (PI/PO/IDM/CRM/EP/MDG/Solman) need a Subsequent Connector on top of the main one — that's BASIS-created; SPML1 is the main connector, SPML2 is the sub-subsequent connector. Not required for straight ABAP systems.
Create a group, then: 2.B.1 assign the connector group to a group type — set the connector group status to Logical Group for AC. 2.B.2 assign the connector(s) you created in Step 1 to this group.
Set the Integration Scenario per connector. AM = Automatic Monitoring (Process Control). The Access Control–relevant ones: AUTH → BRM, PROV → ARM, ROLMG → BRM, SUPMG → EAM.

items.h: 4. Maintain Connector Settings (Path: SPRO → GRC → Access Control)
items.b: Define Application Type, Environment and PSS (Password Self Service).

items.h: 5. Maintain Mapping for Actions and Connector Groups
items.b: 5a. Maintain Connector Group Status — enter the connector group name and make it active. 5b. Assign a default connector to the connector group, per action (Role Generation, Role Risk Analysis, Authorization Maintenance, Provisioning, HR Trigger).

blocks.text: Two rules that matter: under one connector group, only one system can be the Default Connector for a given action — but every system in the group should still be mapped to every action.

topics.title: Access Risk Analysis (ARA)
topics.summary: How ARA performs SoD checks, rule sets and risk reporting.

blocks.text: ARA is the module responsible for risk checks and rule-based analyses.

topics.title: Emergency Access Management (EAM)
topics.summary: How Firefighter IDs grant temporary critical access, and the centralized, decentralized and role-based setups.

blocks.text: EAM (formerly SPM in GRC 5.x, Fire Fighter in VIRSA 4.0) lets users temporarily use elevated 'Firefighter' access for critical, rarely-used transactions — without permanently assigning risky access to their normal ID.

topics.title: Business Role Management (BRM)
topics.summary: How BRM standardizes role creation with a defined methodology, and makes roles visible for access requests via ARM.

blocks.text: BRM (formerly ERM in GRC 5.x, Role Expert in VIRSA 4.0) automates and governs role creation, approval, testing and import — so roles built in the backend become visible and requestable through GRC's access request form (ARM).
